For Main, GJR-GARCH has the lowest QLIKE loss at both horizons, but does not beat EWMA significantly (Diebold-Mariano p = 0.09 at one day, 0.28 at one month).

Across all 10 series, a long 252-session historical window is significantly worse than EWMA in 16 of 20 series-horizon tests (p < 0.05). Only 3 of 100 model-vs-EWMA tests show a significant improvement over EWMA: the big gain comes from reacting to recent volatility at all, not from the choice among conditional models.
GJR-GARCH, which lets falls raise volatility more than rises, has the lowest loss in 6 of 10 series at one day and 5 at one month; its median loss is 0.99x EWMA (1 day) and 1.00x (1 month).

Asset class matters: GJR-GARCH significantly beats EWMA only for Benchmark, VTI (US equity and the VTI-heavy benchmark), consistent with the leverage effect being strongest in equities; on bond ETFs the GARCH-type and HAR models are significantly worse than EWMA in 10 tests (BND, BNDX, IEF, TIP), so a simple EWMA is the safer default for fixed income.

Fixing 99% VaR needs both a responsive volatility model and a fat-tailed distribution. Over 1005 days (expected 10 exceptions): the slow historical windows fail Kupiec's test even with filtered historical simulation (18 and 21 exceptions); the conditional models with a normal quantile fail in 2 of 4 cases; conditional models with filtered historical simulation pass in 4 of 4 (EWMA 12, GJR 13).

One-month Mincer-Zarnowitz slopes are below 1 for every model (0.03 for the 252-day window, 0.64 for the best): no model is fully calibrated, and a year-long window says almost nothing about the next month. Four years containing two sharp episodes is a short sample for ranking models.
Applied as a 10% volatility target without leverage, EWMA forecasts reduced Main's maximum drawdown from -21.4% to -17.2% with almost the same annual return (5.10% vs 5.16%); details on page 4.

With EWMA forecasts the overlay held 90% exposure on average and cut volatility from 11.2% to 9.5%, maximum drawdown from -21.4% to -17.2% and the worst month from -7.5% to -5.4%, while annual return moved from 5.16% to 5.10% (costs 11 bps in total). The Sharpe ratio is essentially unchanged (p = 1.00).

With GJR-GARCH forecasts the same rule earned 4.06% a year with a smaller risk reduction (max drawdown -19.7%); its Sharpe ratio is lower but not significantly (p = 0.27). A model that forecasts slightly better on average did not make the better overlay here, a reminder that forecast accuracy and decision value differ.

A monthly overlay cannot react to a shock inside the month: the highest monthly volatility stays at 28% (April 2025). Four years is far too short to claim the overlay adds value; the evidence is about controlling risk, and later research (Cederburg et al., 2020) finds volatility management rarely improves performance out of sample.
